persona.bio: Kayla, 27, electrician who owns a one truck business in Phoenix. She is in attics by 7am and on job sites all day; she has no office and works from her Samsung phone in the truck. The paperwork around the job is what drags: writing quotes, sending invoices, texting homeowners about times, chasing payment, asking for reviews. She does quotes on her phone at night, often by talking them through. She tried ChatGPT once to write a review request and forgot about it.

steps.firstStep: I’m an electrician who runs my own one truck business, mostly doing homes in Phoenix. I write quotes for customers several times a week and want a quick, clear quote each time. Write a short, plain text quote I can send by text message, with a parts line, a labor line, a total, and a line saying how long the quote is good for. Keep it friendly and under 90 words. Here are the job details: [paste the job details, parts costs, labor hours and the quote’s validity here].

steps.note: I’m an electrician and I run my own one truck business, mostly doing work in homes around Phoenix. I write to homeowners, so I keep things short, friendly and plain. I text most of the time, so a few sentences is usually enough. I like a straight answer with the price or the next step up front. Never add details I did not give you, like a price, a date, a part or a promise. If something is missing, put it in square brackets and leave it for me to fill in. Never use big words or sales talk. Give me one version I can read, fix and send myself.

steps.title: Your quotes, written with AI
steps.read: From now on you tell Claude the job, the parts and the price, and it drafts the quote for you to read. You already know the numbers, so Claude only does the writing and you keep the final say. Every quote comes out in the same plain, clear shape, and you fix anything before it goes to the homeowner.

material.label: Your quote message
items: I’m an electrician running my own one truck business, mostly doing homes in Phoenix. Write a quote I can text or email to a homeowner. Job: [what the work is, like a 200 amp panel swap]. Site notes: [anything that changes the work, like a tight attic and extra labor hours]. Parts: about [parts cost]. Total: [total price]. Good for: [number of days]. Keep it short, friendly and plain, in my voice. Use only the numbers I gave you. Do not add details, promises or prices I did not give. Put anything missing in square brackets. Give me one quote I can read, fix and send, and a one line text I can send with it.

steps.task: Chasing payment and asking for reviews
steps.title: Your payment and review messages, saved once on your phone
steps.read: Your payment and review messages live on your phone’s keyboard, each a few letters away. You type a short shortcut and the full message appears, so you stop writing the same nudge over and over. You still read it, change the name or amount, and then send it.

material.label: Your replies
items: Hi [first name], this is [my name] with [my business]. Just a quick reminder that the invoice for [job] is still open. You can pay at [payment link]. Let me know if you have any questions.
Hi [first name], following up on the invoice for [job], [amount]. It’s past due now. Could you take care of it by [day]? Thank you.
Hi [first name], I want to check in about the invoice for [job]. Is there anything holding it up? I’m happy to answer any questions.
Hi [first name], thanks again for choosing me for [job]. The invoice is here: [payment link]. I appreciate your business.

Hi [first name], it was a pleasure working on your home. If you were happy with the work, would you leave me a quick review? Here’s the link: [review link]. It really helps a small business like mine.
Hi [first name], just a friendly reminder about the review. It only takes a minute here: [review link]. Thank you so much.
Hi [first name], thank you for the payment. I really appreciate it. If you need any more electrical work, just text me.

safeUse: Never type a homeowner’s name, home address, phone number or gate code into Claude. Use square brackets and fill them in yourself.
Never type payment details like card numbers, bank info or a customer’s account numbers.
Check every price, parts count and labor hour in a quote against your own numbers before it goes out.
Check anything about permits, code or inspections against your local rules, because Claude can get these wrong.
Read every message before you send it, and change anything that does not sound like you.

design.today: You write each quote from scratch for the job, and you send about one a day. You text the PDF and call if the homeowner does not answer.
design.newWay: You say the job out loud on your phone, like the panel size, the parts cost and any extra labor, and your saved assistant turns it into a finished quote in your usual wording. You read it, check every number, and then text or email it yourself. The terms and the wording stay the same every time, so you only deal with what is different about the job.

steps.goal: Collect three or four of your past quotes, including the 200 amp panel swap, so the assistant can copy your wording and layout.
Get Claude ready on your phone so you can use it from the truck or the driveway.
Make a project for quotes and add your past quotes so it learns how you write them.
Save instructions so the assistant turns your job details into a quote with the parts, labor, total and 30 day validity, and asks you about anything missing.
Practice describing a job out loud and getting back the finished quote text.

material.label: Quote assistant instructions
material.what: Tells the assistant to write quotes the way you do, with parts, labor, total and how long the price is good for.

material.label: Example quotes
material.what: Your past quotes, including the 200 amp panel swap with the tight attic, as models for wording and layout.

material.label: Job checklist
material.what: The short list of details the assistant asks for when you leave something out, like the parts cost, extra labor and the total.

material.label: Tone notes
material.what: A few lines on how you talk to homeowners, so quotes sound like you and not like a form letter.

design.checkPoint: You read the finished quote and check every number, the parts cost, the labor and the total, before you send it yourself.

design.task: Chasing payment and asking for reviews
design.today: You chase payments and ask for reviews one by one, which takes time. You do it by text, and you work from your phone only.
design.newWay: You keep a few saved replies on your phone for the usual cases, like a first nudge, a firmer reminder and a review request after a finished job. Each one is a few letters away, so you only add the name and the amount. You read it and send it yourself, and the wording stays polite and steady every time.

steps.goal: Decide which messages you send most, like a friendly payment reminder, a second reminder and a review request.
Get ChatGPT ready on your phone to help write the wording.
Save a few lines about you and your business so the messages sound like you.
Save each message on your phone so one short shortcut brings it up for you to fill in and send.

material.label: Review request

material.label: Shortcut list
material.what: The few letters that bring up each saved message, so you remember them.

material.label: About you note
material.what: A few lines on your business and how you speak to homeowners.

design.checkPoint: You fill in the name and amount, read each message, and press send yourself.
